articles.title: The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
articles.text:
The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
What will it take for the Dutch to eat them?
Confronted with a seasoned, boiled, arguably delicious crayfish, some of the people of the Netherlands are not sure exactly what to do. “Do you suck the head out?” I heard from the table next to me earlier this summer, at Two Chefs, a restaurant in Amsterdam that hosts a monthly crayfish boil.
 
 Yes is the answer: The best way to eat a crayfish is to shell the tail, then slurp the flavored juices out of the head, and pick out the remaining meat with your hands.
This strategy might not be an immediate transatlantic hit. At the boil, one 29-year-old from Maastricht likened the meal to shrimp but with more work. Two twins told me that the crayfish would need to look a little more chic on the plate to appeal to the Dutch public. But, given the ever-growing population of crayfish in the Netherlands, coming around to eating more of them could benefit the country.
Because if Dutch consumers aren’t sure how they feel about crayfish, crayfish inarguably love the Netherlands. They have invaded the country’s waterways so thoroughly that they have become a real problem, and dealing with them will mean persuading more creatures—including Dutch people—to eat more crayfish.
The crayfish invasion started decades ago, but in recent years, the red swamp crayfish (also known as the Louisiana crawfish) has become a particular pest, Pim Lemmers, an ecologist at Radboud University who has dedicated his career to researching crayfish, told me. In the 1980s, it was brought to the Netherlands as food, and people naively released the animals into the environment. The waterways in the Netherlands are very interconnected and became a “crayfish highway” of sorts, Ivo Roessink, an aquatic ecotoxicologist at Wageningen University & Research, told me. But crayfish can walk and breathe on land, too, and have been spotted in parks, along bike lanes, and at Schiphol airport, where the birds use the runway to crush them.
And they can dig—burrows up to three feet long that can collapse the edges of fields into the water and that some people fear could damage the country’s extensive system of dams, dikes, and canals. Scientists emphasize that the risk to dams and dikes is low; from their point of view, the bigger risk is to other creatures that live in the water. Crayfish are omnivorous: “They totally destroy underwater vegetation,” Roessink said. They also eat detritus, amphibian and insect larvae, snails and other invertebrates, small fish, and one another—a sight I witnessed for myself.
But crayfish cannibalism will not end the invasion; in fact, although the Netherlands’ central government is working on a program for crayfish management, getting rid of the species will likely be impossible. “I know of one example where they effectively eradicated crayfish, and that was in the U.S.,” Roessink said. “There was an infected pond, and they turned it into a parking lot.” (Resorting to this solution in the Netherlands would require paving over the entire country.) Research in the Netherlands and elsewhere has shown that even extensive trapping won’t necessarily eliminate crayfish. The most anyone can hope for is fewer of them.
Some water boards of the Netherlands are trying to persuade all sorts of creatures to eat more crayfish, including herons, eels, and European catfish, which are themselves something of an invasive threat. And, in theory, one of the crayfish’s most effective predators could be Dutch people.
Stefan van Ekris and Maarten van der Sanden, who are both managing directors at CrawFish Farm Holland, are trying their best to make it happen. This July, I joined them as they put on waders and immersed themselves in irrigation ditches to set and check their crayfish nets in the Groene Hart, or “Green Heart,” of the Netherlands, the thinly populated pastures and peatlands among some of the country’s largest cities. They get paid per kilogram caught—the expedition I joined yielded about 150 kilograms, or 330 pounds, of live crayfish—but this is really a passion project for them. CrawFish Farm Holland is approved to sell live and prepared catch directly to restaurants and other wholesalers, and hopes to sell its crayfish in supermarkets in the next two years. “We’re not cultivating them,” Van der Sanden told me. “We’re fighting them and eating them.”
In America, Van der Sanden pointed out, Louisiana was able to quickly ramp up crayfish production and demand in the 1980s. But the scientists I spoke with were skeptical of this strategy. “You will never eat yourself out of this crisis,” Roessink said. And if people like crayfish too much, Lemmers said, they might start cultivating crayfish in their backyard or trapping them without oversight, which could promote further spread. Even if more Dutch people come around to the pleasures of a messy boil, the crayfish still could come out ahead.

articles.title: Đình chỉ trại vịt 30.000 con ở Thanh Hóa
articles.text:
Ngày 3/9, thông tin từ Văn phòng UBND tỉnh Thanh Hóa cho biết liên quan phản ánh của Báo Tiền Phong về trang trại vịt hơn 30.000 con ở xã Nông Cống gây mùi hôi, ô nhiễm, ảnh hưởng đời sống người dân, Phó Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Cao Văn Cường đã có chỉ đạo, yêu cầu cơ sở chăn nuôi vi phạm dừng hoạt động chăn nuôi, khắc phục các vi phạm môi trường còn tồn tại.
Theo đó, sau khi Sở Nông nghiệp và Môi trường kiểm tra, báo cáo về các vi phạm tại 2 dự án trang trại nuôi vịt xiêm do ông Lê Quang Hòa quản lý, vận hành ở xã Nông Cống, UBND tỉnh yêu cầu các cơ sở này phải hoàn thành việc xuất bán toàn bộ đàn vịt và dừng hoàn toàn hoạt động chăn nuôi để tổ chức rà soát, khắc phục triệt để các tồn tại về bảo vệ môi trường.
Việc thực hiện chỉ đạo chậm nhất đến hết 15/9.
Trong thời gian này, cơ sở không được nhập đàn, tái đàn hoặc tái chăn nuôi khi chưa hoàn thành việc khắc phục, hoàn thiện các thủ tục pháp lý và chưa được cơ quan chức năng xác nhận đủ điều kiện hoạt động.
UBND tỉnh cũng yêu cầu từ nay đến 15/9, cơ sở phải thực hiện vệ sinh chuồng trại hằng ngày, thu gom, xử lý chất thải, vận hành liên tục hệ thống phun nước dạng sương có sử dụng chế phẩm vi sinh để giảm mùi hôi, khẩn trương khắc phục các vị trí lưới bị bong, rách, duy trì hệ thống chắn, hệ thống thông gió và các công trình, biện pháp kiểm soát mùi.
Sau khi xuất bán toàn bộ đàn vịt, cơ sở phải tổng vệ sinh, tiêu độc, khử trùng toàn bộ khu vực chuồng trại; thu gom, xử lý toàn bộ phân, nước thải và các loại chất thải phát sinh, không để tồn đọng, rò rỉ, phát tán mùi hôi hoặc xả chất thải chưa được xử lý đạt quy chuẩn ra môi trường.
Phó Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Thanh Hóa cũng giao UBND xã Nông Cống rà soát hồ sơ về bảo vệ môi trường, đất đai, xây dựng, chăn nuôi và các hồ sơ pháp lý liên quan đối với cơ sở. Tăng cường kiểm tra, giám sát chặt chẽ việc thực hiện các yêu cầu, bảo đảm cơ sở hoàn thành việc xuất bán toàn bộ đàn vịt và dừng hoạt động chăn nuôi của đơn vị vi phạm.
Trước đó, người dân thôn Vạn Thắng (xã Nông Cống) phản ánh từ năm 2023, khi trang trại chăn nuôi vịt của Công ty TNHH Grimaud bắt đầu hoạt động, mùi hôi từ khu vực chăn nuôi thường xuyên ảnh hưởng đến khu dân cư, đặc biệt khi thời tiết thay đổi, gió đưa mùi từ trang trại vào nhà dân.
Đại diện Phòng Kinh tế xã Nông Cống cho biết trang trại chăn nuôi vịt này có diện tích khoảng 2 ha, quy mô 60.000 con. Xã Nông Cống từng nhiều lần lập biên bản, xử lý vì trại vịt gây mùi hôi, ô nhiễm và yêu cầu khắc phục. Phòng kinh tế và lực lượng công an xã Nông Cống đã đến làm việc với đơn vị quản lý trại nuôi vịt. Tại thời điểm kiểm tra, trang trại còn khoảng 30.000 con vịt.
Lãnh đạo UBND tỉnh Thanh Hóa sau đó đã giao Sở Nông nghiệp và Môi trường chủ trì, phối hợp với công an tỉnh, UBND xã Nông Cống và các đơn vị có liên quan kiểm tra, xác minh.

articles.title: What the Floods Say About Xi Jinping
articles.text:
What the Floods Say About Xi Jinping
China’s leader behaves more like an emperor than a man of the people.
When the Yangtze River flooded in 1998 and inundated villages in central China, Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party’s general secretary, was on the scene, bullhorn in hand, to encourage local relief efforts. Ten years later, his successor, Hu Jintao, stood among the rubble after an earthquake rocked Sichuan province, in the country’s southwest. Last week, after floodwaters caused by a collapsing glacier tore through the Himalayas between Nepal and China, leaving more than 1,100 people dead and thousands more missing, the party’s current general secretary, Xi Jinping, stayed largely and safely in Beijing.
In the United States, where politicians have to worry about the needs and feelings of voters, elected representatives are expected to be more visible and engaged in national crises. In 2021, Republican Senator Ted Cruz earned public condemnation when he was caught absconding to Mexico while Texas suffered a deep freeze and power outages. As a Communist dictator, Xi doesn’t have to fret over public-approval ratings. Yet his absence signals a bigger problem for China: Xi has become so powerful that he has lost touch with the country he governs.
Despite being professed Marxists, China’s leaders rarely interact with the working class. But Xi at least used to try to seem like a man of the people. In 2013, about a year into his tenure, Chinese media made a big deal out of his visit to a steamed-bun restaurant in Beijing; the state-owned China Daily praised him for showing his “common touch.”
Today, there’s nothing common about Xi Jinping. He has amassed greater personal power than any other Chinese leader since Mao Zedong, the Communist regime’s founder, who died half a century ago. To justify his outsize role in China’s government, Xi’s tireless propagandists portray him as something grander than a party boss: a philosopher king, whose doctrine of wisdom, called Xi Jinping Thought, is meant to be both studied and obeyed. He is the great global statesman, guiding foreign policy into a new era of peace and prosperity. His various “global initiatives” outline his vision for a reformed world order.
Mere mortals such as Jiang and Hu had to stomp around muddy disaster zones to prove their worth. But Xi “does not need to go to steam-bun shops to pretend he is with the people any longer, or, for that matter, to be visible when a major disaster has happened,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute at the University of London, told me. “He no doubt thinks and therefore acts as if he is above all.”
In Xi’s calculus, the Himalayan communities destroyed by the floods are hardly worthy of his attention. The area in question is part of Tibet, a region that borders Nepal and was once independent. Xi has demonstrated a persistent hostility toward China’s minorities, who, in their stubborn resistance to Chinese civilization, threaten his vision of national unity. A new law that took effect in July aims to transform Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongolians, and other minorities into properly loyal citizens by forcing them to adopt the majority Han Chinese culture. Until the Tibetans fall in line, “there is not really a compelling reason for him to visit them just because a disaster struck,” Tsang argued.
From Xi’s perspective, appearing at the scene of the floods would have involved more risk than reward. A purportedly all-knowing and all-seeing leader can’t make mistakes or even be associated with bad news, so Xi has good reason to avoid potentially tarnishing himself with an uncertain rescue operation. The politically safer option involves managing the crisis from afar while dispatching others to get their hands dirty. Beijing is also carefully controlling the information coming from the disaster zone. International journalists are already barred from Tibet, so any news about the disaster and the relief effort is from Chinese state sources. The state-run news agency Xinhua duly announced on Friday that Xi chaired a meeting of the party’s powerful Politburo to “deliberate and make arrangements on rescue and relief efforts.”
The China-focused research firm Trivium noted that Xi’s response to the floods was in keeping with his usual approach to disasters, which is to visit long after the crisis has passed and the rebuilding has begun. Xi is “keeping himself above operational risk” and is focused on “owning the recovery rather than the chaos,” Trivium’s report said. Xi may at some point decide to show up on the ground, but probably well after the initial chaos has subsided.
The stories and images from the floods have moved hearts, but Xi has bigger things to think about than a mudslide on the far edge of his empire. One of his priorities has been to reshape Chinese culture by merging the party’s beloved Marxism with traditional Confucianism. Although that effort appears to have had little traction with the public, Xi himself seems to have taken these ideas to heart. He may speak like a socialist, but he governs more like an emperor, deserving of national veneration and shielded from scrutiny. But many emperors were remote figures, removed from the real world behind the walls of the Forbidden City, and reliant on courtiers for news from outside. As Xi’s absence from the flooding disaster demonstrates, he, too, has become detached from the daily struggles and sentiments of his citizens—and unresponsive to the nation’s mounting economic and social problems as a result.
How the Chinese people feel about Xi’s response is impossible to know. Assiduous censors deter candor and cleanse social-media platforms of any direct criticism. Perhaps life in an authoritarian political system breeds a practical indifference, given that people have no influence over who rules them anyway. But with a spare few hours on the ground among those who just lost everything, Xi could have at least shown that he cares. His loyal public has surely noticed that even that was too much.

articles.title: Thủ tướng: Tiếp tục triển khai chính sách miễn, giảm thuế, phí
articles.text:
Chiều 3/9, phát biểu kết luận phiên họp Chính phủ thường kỳ tháng 8, Thủ tướng nêu rõ đây là thời điểm chúng ta cần tăng tốc, bứt phá, quyết tâm cao nhất để đạt mục tiêu đề ra.
Trong bối cảnh tình hình thế giới và khu vực tiếp tục diễn biến phức tạp, khó lường, tiềm ẩn nhiều rủi ro, Thủ tướng đánh giá, Chính phủ đã nỗ lực tập trung hoàn thiện thể chế, cải thiện môi trường đầu tư kinh doanh, ổn định kinh tế vĩ mô, kiểm soát lạm phát, bảo đảm các cân đối lớn của nền kinh tế, đẩy mạnh giải ngân vốn đầu tư công, phát triển hạ tầng, thúc đẩy tăng trưởng kinh tế…
Bên cạnh những kết quả đạt được, Thủ tướng cũng chỉ ra những tồn tại, hạn chế như giải ngân vốn đầu tư công ở một số bộ và dự án trọng điểm chưa có nhiều chuyển biến tích cực, các dự án còn gặp khó khăn trong giải phóng mặt bằng, thiếu nguồn cung vật liệu và lao động, chi phí tăng cao. Thúc đẩy xuất khẩu, giảm nhập siêu, hoạt động thị trường tài chính, tiền tệ, tín dụng còn đối mặt sức ép...
Phấn đấu giảm lãi suất cho vay
Về nhiệm vụ thời gian tới, Thủ tướng yêu cầu các bộ, cơ quan, địa phương thường xuyên rà soát, cập nhật kịch bản tăng trưởng theo từng tháng, từng quý; chủ động nhận diện những điểm nghẽn ảnh hưởng đến mục tiêu tăng trưởng để tập trung tháo gỡ.
Bộ Tài chính tiếp tục triển khai hiệu quả các chính sách miễn, giảm, gia hạn thuế, phí, lệ phí để hỗ trợ người dân, doanh nghiệp; rà soát quy trình hoàn thuế giá trị gia tăng (GTGT) đối với hàng xuất khẩu theo hướng tăng cường phân loại rủi ro, đẩy nhanh xử lý các hồ sơ của doanh nghiệp chấp hành tốt pháp luật, giảm chi phí về thời gian; tăng cường các biện pháp chống chuyển giá.
Với Ngân hàng Nhà nước Việt Nam, lãnh đạo Chính phủ yêu cầu tiếp tục điều hành chính sách tiền tệ chủ động, linh hoạt; tập trung tín dụng vào các lĩnh vực ưu tiên, các dự án trọng điểm.
Thủ tướng lưu ý cần thường xuyên đánh giá “điểm cân bằng” giữa yêu cầu kiểm soát lạm phát và hỗ trợ tăng trưởng, xác định ngưỡng cảnh báo; chủ động sử dụng các công cụ thuộc thẩm quyền để phát huy tối đa hiệu quả chính sách, giữ ổn định thanh khoản, phấn đấu giảm lãi suất cho vay.
Đặc biệt, người đứng đầu Chính phủ yêu cầu Ngân hàng Nhà nước điều hành linh hoạt tiền gửi Kho bạc Nhà nước tại ngân hàng Nhà nước và các ngân hàng thương mại để tăng thanh khoản cho nền kinh tế; chỉ đạo các tổ chức tín dụng tăng cường hợp tác với các quỹ đầu tư và các định chế tài chính nhằm đa dạng hóa các nguồn vốn cho doanh nghiệp.
Với Bộ Công Thương, Thủ tướng yêu cầu bảo đảm ổn định nguồn cung năng lượng, cung ứng đủ điện cho sản xuất, kinh doanh và sinh hoạt; khẩn trương hoàn thiện phương án về hệ thống phân phối xăng dầu; tháo gỡ dứt điểm khó khăn, vướng mắc, sớm khôi phục hoạt động các nhà máy sản xuất xăng sinh học, đẩy nhanh tiến độ các dự án điện, dầu khí trọng điểm.
Bộ Giáo dục và Đào tạo phối hợp với các đơn vị liên quan bảo đảm tốt chế độ, chính sách đối với học sinh thuộc diện chính sách, yếu thế, có hoàn cảnh khó khăn, học sinh vùng đồng bào dân tộc thiểu số, vùng khó khăn; rà soát ngay việc cung ứng, bảo đảm sách giáo khoa, nhất là tại những nơi khó khăn.

articles.title: Should We Be Afraid of Our Food?
articles.text:
Should We Be Afraid of Our Food?
America's food-safety system is being methodically dismantled by the Trump administration.
The cyclosporiasis outbreak that has garnered so much attention in recent months is unquestionably bad news. People have been sickened in at least 48 states, and the number of lab-confirmed cases—about 17,000—represents only a fraction of the number of people who have been infected by the parasite.
But as foodborne illnesses go, a cyclospora infection—most likely caused in this instance by the consumption of iceberg lettuce contaminated with human feces—is relatively mild: unpleasant but rarely life-threatening. The two people who have died during the current outbreak had serious underlying conditions. Other foodborne pathogens are far more dangerous. More than 1 million Americans are sickened by Salmonella every year; invasive, potentially life-threatening infections occur in about 8 percent of lab-confirmed cases, and cause meningitis, sepsis, and other serious complications. A botulism infection can cause paralysis, seizures, nerve damage, lung damage, and brain damage, as well as death.
A few years ago, I reported here on an outbreak of Cronobacter infections linked to powdered infant formula and the subsequent recall by Abbott Nutrition. Two recent botulism outbreaks linked to powdered infant formula made by two other companies have thus far received little attention. During an outbreak that peaked in November 2025, at least 48 infants across 17 states were stricken with botulism traced to powdered formula from the company ByHeart. The infants were hospitalized with severe complications; one of them suffered multiple strokes. Then, earlier this year, at least four infants in three states were stricken with botulism from powdered formula made by the company Nara Organics. All four infants were hospitalized.
A key ingredient in the tainted formula sold by both companies was milk powder from a common supplier—the likely carrier of the botulism spores. Today’s powdered formula is highly industrialized, with dozens of ingredients from multiple sources. The contents of a single can of formula may contain milk from thousands of different cows. Nobody has ever fed babies this kind of stuff before. From December 2025 through February 2026, more than 100 infants in at least 10 countries were sickened in all likelihood by powdered formula tainted with spores from the bacterium Bacillus cereus. The formula, manufactured by several different companies, including Nestlé and Danone, had been contaminated by a fatty-acid additive supplied by a biotech firm in Wuhan, China.
A generation ago, an outbreak of food poisoning generally remained small-scale. The source was likely to be tainted ground beef from a local butcher shop or an egg salad gone bad at a church picnic. As the scale of industrial food production has grown, so has the scale of foodborne outbreaks. When I wrote my book Fast Food Nation, published in 2001, high levels of fecal contamination of ground beef were already a nationwide problem, not just a local one, because huge ground-beef-processing plants with poor safety procedures were supplying the fast-food industry.
The dairy industry now presents similar problems of scale. The supply chain for the botulism-tainted infant formula went like this: 55 dairies in California sold raw milk to a company called Organic West; that raw milk was then shipped from California to an enormous plant operated by Dairy Farmers of America in Fallon, Nevada, and processed into milk powder. For ByHeart, the powder was shipped to a plant in Iowa, turned into formula, shipped to Oregon for additional processing, packaged there, and sold throughout the United States. For Nara Organics, the milk powder was shipped from Nevada to Germany, manufactured into formula, shipped to Denmark, packaged, and shipped back to the U.S.
Government never adapts quickly, and because policies are adopted piecemeal over decades, many federal food-safety rules make little sense. For instance, frozen cheese pizzas are regulated by the FDA—but if a frozen pizza has a lot of pepperoni or other meats, it’s regulated by the Department of Agriculture. The U.S. is the only developed country that divides responsibility for food safety among separate government agencies. So it is hardly surprising that monitoring and enforcement have not kept up with changes in food production. The larger problem is that the food-safety system we have—underfunded for decades—is being methodically dismantled by the Trump administration.
The FDA is responsible for the safety of about 80 percent of the food consumed in the United States. Last year, James Jones, the highly respected head of the FDA’s human-foods division, resigned from his post, citing the “indiscriminate” firing of 89 staff members. The loss of such expertise threatens to cripple the agency’s food-safety efforts. Kyle Diamantas—who replaced Jones and now serves as the acting head of the FDA—has no scientific, medical, or public-health training. He is an attorney (and Donald Trump Jr.’s hunting companion). While employed at the law firm Jones Day, Diamantas defended Abbott Laboratories in a lawsuit alleging that the company had knowingly sold infant formula that could cause severe bowel problems. Abbott lost the suit and in August agreed to pay a $670 million settlement to resolve that case and other claims. In a statement to investors, Abbott said that the settlement is “not in any way an admission of liability” and that the company “remains confident in the safety of these products.”
The USDA, which has food-safety oversight of meat, eggs, and poultry, has also suffered significant cutbacks under Donald Trump, losing about one-fifth of its workforce in 2025. At the CDC, the chief food-safety expert, Daniel Jernigan, resigned in August 2025, angered by budget cuts and political interference. The number of pathogens tracked by FoodNet, a crucial CDC surveillance program, has been cut by 75 percent. The amount of money spent on FoodNet annually is a fraction of what has already been spent to renovate the Reflecting Pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial.
During the late 1890s, tainted and adulterated food was commonplace in the United States. Upton Sinclair’s muckraking 1906 novel, The Jungle, exposed a variety of noxious practices—such as making sausage from rats—and prompted President Theodore Roosevelt to support food-safety legislation. The food industry vehemently opposed Roosevelt: “We are paying all we care to pay,” one executive told Congress. The industry lost that battle—federal agencies gained regulatory power—but continues to fight back. It spends more on lobbying and political donations than the oil or defense industries do.
The tragedy is that public-health experts agree on many of the straightforward steps that should be taken to ensure food safety. And they can point to a record of success. In 2002, a year after the publication of Fast Food Nation, I met a woman named Barbara Kowalcyk, whose 2-year-old son, Kevin, had recently died after being infected with E. coli O157:H7 from a tainted hamburger. It was an all-too-frequent occurrence back then—nationwide outbreaks of E. coli O157:H7 were routinely caused by ground beef. Kowalcyk was determined that other parents should never have to endure her experience. Trained as a biostatistician, she returned to school and earned a doctorate in environmental science and food safety. She is now a professor at George Washington University’s school of public health. A decade after we met, Kowalcyk played a leading role in campaigning for “test and hold,” a food-safety rule to prevent meat companies from shipping ground beef until it had tested negative for dangerous forms of E. coli. In 2013, the rule was finally adopted by the USDA. Few large E. coli outbreaks are today caused by ground beef.
Similar test-and-hold rules could help eliminate Salmonella from poultry. A 2022 study by Consumer Reports found that almost one-third of the ground chicken sold at American supermarkets contained Salmonella—an extraordinarily high level. Strict food-safety regulation of the poultry industry in Denmark has reduced the level of Salmonella contamination in broiler chickens there from 14 to 0.3 percent—and, as a result, the number of people sickened by Salmonella has declined by 99.6 percent. But the Trump administration recently blocked the adoption of a new rule, about to go in effect after years of deliberation at the USDA, that would have prohibited the sale of poultry products highly contaminated with Salmonella, claiming the rule would have imposed “significant financial and operational burdens on American businesses and consumers.” The Meat Institute and the National Chicken Council backed the move.
When it comes to food manufactured for infants, the federal government has enormous leverage that is going unused. The infant-formula industry is highly concentrated. Two companies, Abbott and Mead Johnson, control more than 80 percent of the market. Through the USDA’s Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children, or WIC, the federal government buys more than half of the infant formula consumed in the United States—meaning that it could swiftly mandate changes on behalf of infant health. But it hasn’t. The Republican-controlled Congress has refused to hold hearings on the botulism outbreaks or on legislation introduced in March that would expand pathogen testing of infant formula and strengthen congressional oversight. The idea of putting all federal food-safety efforts under one roof is a nonstarter.
“We are paying all we care to pay”—that was the industry response in 1906, and that is the response today. It’s the rest of us who bear the cost.

articles.title: Tuyên Quang: Tìm thấy nạn nhân mất tích tại thác Khâu Làn sau hơn 30 giờ tìm kiếm
articles.text:
Không quản vất vả, hiểm nguy, cán bộ, chiến sĩ Cảnh sát phòng cháy, chữa cháy và cứu nạn, cứu hộ Công an tỉnh Tuyên Quang kiên trì bám hiện trường, khẩn trương triển khai các phương án tìm kiếm.
Đến khoảng 14h ngày 3/9, sau hơn 30 giờ nỗ lực tìm kiếm, lực lượng cứu nạn, cứu hộ đã tìm thấy nạn nhân mất tích tại khu vực thác Khâu Làn, xã Quản Bạ.
Trước đó, khoảng 19h30 ngày 1/9, Phòng Cảnh sát phòng cháy, chữa cháy và cứu nạn, cứu hộ Công an tỉnh Tuyên Quang tiếp nhận tin báo từ Công an xã Quản Bạ về việc hai khách du lịch xuống tắm tại thác Khâu Làn.
Trong quá trình tắm, anh Q.T.Đ (sinh năm 1996, trú tại thành phố Hồ Chí Minh) không may bị đuối nước, cuốn vào khu vực hang của thác và mất tích.
Ngay sau khi tiếp nhận thông tin, Phòng Cảnh sát phòng cháy, chữa cháy và cứu nạn, cứu hộ đã chỉ đạo Đội Chữa cháy và cứu nạn, cứu hộ khu vực Hà Giang khẩn trương điều động 12 cán bộ, chiến sĩ cùng phương tiện, thiết bị chuyên dụng đến hiện trường.
Do thác Khâu Làn nằm sâu trong khu vực địa hình núi rừng hiểm trở, việc tiếp cận hiện trường mất nhiều thời gian. Ngay khi tiếp cận hiện trường, lực lượng cứu nạn, cứu hộ nhanh chóng phối hợp với Công an xã Quản Bạ cùng các lực lượng tại chỗ triển khai tìm kiếm.
Công tác tìm kiếm gặp nhiều khó khăn do nước từ thượng nguồn đổ về lớn, dòng thác chảy xiết, khu vực chân thác có nhiều tảng đá phủ rêu trơn trượt, xen kẽ các khe và hốc sâu. Vị trí nạn nhân bị cuốn vào nằm gần khu vực hang, nơi nước đổ mạnh, tầm nhìn hạn chế nên lực lượng cứu nạn, cứu hộ rất khó quan sát và tiếp cận.
Sau hơn 30 giờ nỗ lực tìm kiếm, lực lượng cứu nạn cứu hộ đã tìm thấy nạn nhân mất tích tại thác Khâu Làn, xã Quản Bạ.

articles.title: Hà Nội chính thức có 'Bản đồ mưa ngập'
articles.text:
Điểm đáng chú ý của công cụ này là khả năng cập nhật tình trạng mưa, ngập theo thời gian thực và chủ động gửi cảnh báo đến điện thoại của người dùng.
Mini App "Bản đồ mưa ngập" là một tiện ích chuyên sâu được phát triển đồng bộ và nhúng trực tiếp vào hệ sinh thái iHanoi. Thay vì sử dụng các nguồn tin tản mát trên mạng xã hội, mini app khai thác nguồn dữ liệu chính thống từ hệ thống quan trắc của Công ty TNHH MTV Thoát nước Hà Nội (HSDC).
Với mô hình "tất cả trong một", người dùng iHanoi có thể tiếp cận thông tin ngay lập tức mà không cần cài đặt thêm ứng dụng rời, tối ưu hóa dung lượng thiết bị và thời gian truy cập.
Mini app mang lại trải nghiệm trực quan với các nhóm tính năng được thiết kế cá nhân hóa. Cụ thể, bản đồ trực quan thời gian thực giúp người dùng có thể sử dụng nút chọn "Lọc lớp hiển thị" để chọn xem trạm đo mưa/điểm ngập lụt và linh hoạt chuyển đổi giữa bản đồ nền riêng của Hà Nội hoặc Google Maps (vệ tinh, giao thông) để định vị chính xác nhất. Hệ thống sử dụng thang chỉ thị màu từ xanh (an toàn) đến tím (nghiêm trọng lượng mưa > 1.000mm hoặc ngập sâu >10m).
Khi chạm vào một điểm mưa/ngập cụ thể trên bản đồ, ứng dụng hiển thị Popup chi tiết (tên điểm, địa chỉ, lượng mưa, mức độ ngập). Tính năng này cho phép người dân ngay lập tức thiết lập lộ trình di chuyển an toàn để tránh vùng nguy hiểm.
Người dùng có quyền thiết lập loại cảnh báo, bán kính cảnh báo từ 1km đến 100km và khung giờ nhận cảnh báo. Thông báo đẩy (Push notification) sẽ được gửi tự động theo cấu hình cài đặt người dùng thiết lập.

articles.title: Creating the Perfect Female Monster
articles.text:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
The breakout crime drama Furious opens with a scene that’s hard to watch: Catherine, a serial killer played by Lola Petticrew, is keeping a man prisoner in a row house and taunting him as he dies: “I don’t like the sounds you’re making.” The show’s creator, Liz Meriwether, is announcing right away that you will be spending time with a monster, and the discomfort amps up from there. As the show progresses, we learn that Catherine has been trafficked, and the men she is killing were involved in her abuse.
In an era when “Epstein Island” exists, Catherine represents a specific kind of psychopathic serial killer. She is, as the title suggests, one of the Furies exacting revenge in a world that hasn’t managed to execute justice for her the legal way.
Meriwether says she did not set out to make a statement on the state of female rage or American justice, or even a commentary on Epstein, yet the show may have hit a nerve because those issues are so alive right now. Nine years ago, women’s anger fueled the MeToo movement, and it seemed as if the way society confronts sexual harassment and abuse was on the brink of transformation. “Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been,” the Atlantic staff writer Sophie Gilbert says. “And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb.”
In this episode, Meriwether talks about the complications of humanizing a serial killer and how the project of creating complicated women characters has evolved in her decade of writing for television. And Gilbert talks about what it means that more women creators are owning the stories told about women.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Hanna Rosin: A female monster is a rare but recurring creature. She often emerges at moments in history when women in society are collectively angry at the powers that be but unable to express it. Maybe they’re too defeated or maybe numb, so the monster gets revenge for them.
I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic.
Right now, there is a particularly interesting monster out there taking revenge on a fictional Jeffrey Epstein. It’s playing out on the Hulu show Furious—the season finale aired this week.
Sophie Gilbert: Well, it was one of those shows that became a slow burn, I think.
[Theme song from Furious]
Rosin: This is staff writer Sophie Gilbert.
Gilbert: When it first debuted, there wasn’t that much chatter about it. But then you started to see people watch, and it became this word-of-mouth hit.
Rosin: Furious is a dark and sometimes disturbing TV show about a female serial killer, played by Lola Petticrew, who is pursued by a female FBI agent, played by Emmy Rossum.
Gilbert: So there’s a lot about it that is quite kind of tropey, old-school procedural. It’s a crime show. The cop and the killer being pursued, they have that kind of, Oh, we’re not so different, you and I, kind of thing going on.
But at the same time, it was also like no other procedural I’ve ever seen, in the sense that in so many crime shows, you see women’s bodies used like window dressing almost. And this is a show that really seems to be made about women, not for women necessarily, but it’s interested in women. It’s interested in what happens to women when they go through traumatic experiences, what happens to women when they become angry. There’s so much that is kind of really deep and tied to these mythological elements of transformation and violence. And it just works well on so many levels.
Rosin: The show’s mythological elements are in the name. It’s called Furious after the Furies, the Greek goddesses of vengeance. In the show, the Furies are implied to be serial killer Catherine, FBI agent Alice, and Alice’s mentor, Nora—three women who, in different ways, have all failed to find the justice they need.
Gilbert: So Nora Washington is the head of the FBI’s sex-crimes unit in the show. She’s played by Quincy Tyler Bernstine in this extraordinary performance. She’s so good. And she has a few speeches where she’s talking to Alice Black, sort of the main character in the show, who’s played by Emmy Rossum, who is trying to become an FBI agent under her wing. And she’s explaining to her the toll that this job takes, of looking into these horrendous sex crimes, these crimes often against underage girls, against children.
You take on this responsibility when you do this job of doing this thing that no one else will do, to try and achieve a measure of justice, or certainly a measure of justice that is often impossible, and it changes you.
Quincy Tyler Bernstine (as Nora Washington in Furious): Everyone likes it when there’s a sweet little woman lying on the floor, naked and cut up in pieces. I get so fucking angry.
Gilbert: Because you have to become, in some ways, a monster to do this day after day.
Bernstine: It doesn’t matter, anything you do. The ones who are really to blame don’t get caught. Never. Never.
Gilbert: So there are all these sort of elemental themes of Greek tragedy and Greek drama that seem to come through.
Bernstine: You think you’re ever gonna catch anyone who matters?
Gilbert: So this show starts with a scene of a woman whose name we later find out is Catherine—she’s played by Lola Petticrew—who is keeping a man prisoner in a Brooklyn row house on Halloween.
[Sounds from Furious]
Gilbert: And Catherine is wearing a mask, and she is eating candy corn, and she is clearly torturing this man. And then eventually, we see her murder him.
Lola Petticrew (as Catherine Grace in Furious): I don’t really like listening to you. I don’t like the sounds you’re making.
Gilbert: And the show begins in this really stark way of saying, This is who this character is. Like, Be horrified by this; be appalled by her actions. It’s sort of really uncomfortable to watch in lots of ways, really visceral. And then as the show goes on, you understand more about who she is. You understand her history. You understand why she’s doing what she’s doing, her flawed but in some ways very sympathetic logic. And you see her full humanity. And she becomes, yes, a serial killer, but one who does seem to be doing it for reasons that are, if not fully justifiable, you start to sort of empathize with them a little bit more.
Rosin: Yeah. And here’s the difficult thing: The parallels to the current world are apparent. This is essentially a Jeffrey Epstein setup. It’s a setup about people who are portrayed as rich. There’s a man at the center of it. There’s a sort of a twisted luring in of teenagers and young women. It really has obvious parallels to the world we are currently living in. And here’s a woman exacting justice because the justice system wouldn’t.
Gilbert: Yes.
Rosin: So as I describe it, it is sympathetic. You are, in some ways, supposed to root for this person who at the very first scene is gruesome.
Gilbert: I don’t know if you’re supposed to root for her, but it becomes impossible not to, in some ways.
Rosin: Yeah, yeah.
Gilbert: And I think that’s part of the trick. The show is not black and white morally. It reveals things, and it explains them, and it offers context for them. And we, as human beings, watch it, and we have our own context, and we have our own life experiences, and we add. And we’re supposed to make our own judgments, but I don’t think the show is telling us what to sort of presume one way or another. And that, to me, is what makes it so interesting as an experience.
But yes, this character Jay Easton is, obviously—he’s certainly in the Jeffrey Epstein mold. He’s a billionaire. He’s revealed to have preyed on hundreds, maybe thousands of young, underage women. And yet, what again is striking about the show is that he’s not really interesting. He’s not a character who the show is sort of interested in delving into, really. The show is much more curious about the impact he’s had on the lives of women and girls, and that, I think, is often what goes underplayed or what is missing in our Epstein discourse as well. So it’s shining a light on a different facet of this very topical issue.
[Music]
Rosin: As I watched episode after episode, I had a very uncomfortable reaction that I’m guessing other people had, that the creator of the show, Liz Meriwether—who we’ll talk to later—says she intended: I was not, not rooting for the serial killer, this deeply unlikable, twisted, dark, criminal young woman who was effectively hunting down the men who had abused her when she was a teenager.
Gilbert: Without being, like, morally endorsing murder, it can be cathartic to see where they go with it and to imagine what happens when there’s no justice possible. What do you do with all that rage?
Rosin: Sophie wrote about the show recently for The Atlantic, about how the grief, anger, and rage in Furious reminded her of a different time, nearly a decade ago, when similar feelings of anger generated headlines, spawned think pieces and hashtags, and started the MeToo movement that ultimately fizzled out.
Rosin: Yeah. So what does that reflect in the culture then? A sense of frustration, helplessness? What does that mean?
Gilbert: For me, the show really resonated when I was thinking about—first of all, it’s been almost a decade since the MeToo moment, which is just wild to think about anyway, all this time. But when you think about what happened at the end of 2017, the revelations about Harvey Weinstein, the revelations about all these men—
Reporter (from ABC News): New Yorker magazine reporting new claims of sexual harassment, assault, and rape. One of his accusers going to police, secretly recording her confrontation with Weinstein, but no charges were ever filed.
Gilbert: —there was so much in the sense that we were in this moment of societal transformation and women’s anger. There were so many books written about women’s anger. There were TV shows written about women’s anger. It seemed like rage and fury, and righteous fury, was this great theme in our culture that might have a kind of revolutionary force, that it might help upend systems and overturn injustice.
Reporter (from CBS Miami): Instead of naming one person, Time magazine named its 2017 Person of the Year the “silence breakers,” the name given to the women who came forward to report sexual harassment and assault, sparking the MeToo movement.
Gilbert: And then you look nine years later and you think, Wow, actually, none of that has happened. We’ve, if anything, lost rights. Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been. More and more injustices and horrific crimes against women and girls are revealed. I mean, really, it feels almost daily. We have an overtly misogynist president, I would say. And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb, I think.
And so what this show is doing, which really connected with my own sense of just being unable to feel that rage day after day after day, is wondering what happens when it becomes something else, when it takes a different direction, when it realizes that justice is impossible, and so vengeance is the next best thing.
Rosin: Hmm.
I wanna ask about the broad sweep of things. In your book, Girl on Girl, the thesis is that pop culture taught Millennial women to hate themselves, or maybe just that pop culture of the ’90s and aughts hated women in a certain way. This is a show conceived of by women, written by women, in which a woman and the Furies do get revenge. Does that at least agency, even if it’s a perverse agency, does that represent something different, like controlling the narrative?
Gilbert: Yes, the stories that we get now about women, about the complexities of their lives, the conditions that they’re living under, like the truth of their experience, are made by women about women.
There’s so much that is so much better than it was even 10 years ago. And I was reading an interview with Liz Meriwether, the creator of Furious, where she said—because she’s the creator of a much-beloved sitcom, one of my favorites, called New Girl—and she was mentioning the notes that she got from Fox in terms of sort of making the character more likable and making it broadly more appealing to men, and how now, making this show, Furious, there was none of that.
There’s much more appetite I think, or at least more understanding on the part of people commissioning work like this, that you can be interested in women as a subject and that will make great art that will connect with viewers and be enough of a justification. We don’t need to always be kind of shushing women in a way.
Rosin: Yeah. And it’s not just, you can be interested in women. You can be interested—I mean, the task she’s setting out for a viewer here is: You can be interested in a woman who’s, like you said, a monster. From the very first scene, she’s the exact opposite of a beautiful dead victim. She couldn’t be less likable, at least in the very beginning.
Gilbert: Yes. And the show really trusts us as audiences to see that and to keep watching, which I think is fascinating all on its own. Like, there’s this idea that we don’t need to be coddled into finding this woman cute and sexy. (Laughs.)
Rosin: Yeah.
Gilbert: We can see what she is and we can be hooked anyway, because we’re sophisticated enough consumers of media to understand that the payoff might be worth it.
[Music]
Rosin: After the break, we talk to the Furious showrunner, Liz Meriwether, about why she created a monster you don’t necessarily hate.
[Break]
[Music]
Rosin: Liz Meriwether started as a comedy writer. As Sophie mentioned, her breakout hit was New Girl. Then she wrote The Dropout, a show about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes—also not a classic lovable type. And then Dying for Sex, about a woman who has a terminal-cancer diagnosis—so potentially a perfect victim—but instead, she decides to spend her final months having a lot of sex.
We’ve talked a lot on this episode about post-MeToo progress being stalled. But this—this creation, by female writers, of female characters who test the bounds of likability—is also a kind of progress. I talk to Meriwether—who is in the writers’ room working on Season 2 of Furious—about how her ability to write female characters exactly how she wants them has evolved.
[Music]
Rosin: So the terrible word that’s imposed on female characters forever, which is likable—female politicians, everybody, likability. From the very first scene, you make the decision to make Catherine not likable. Did you get any pushback on that? Like, Put some woman in there who is more pure, or a sort of more recognizable person you can attach yourself to?
Meriwether: As somebody who’s been doing this for about 15 years now, and when I first started doing it, got that note all the time, I was surprised that I didn’t get that note.
Rosin: Can you actually talk about that? ’Cause you were mostly known as a comedy writer. New Girl was the breakout hit, and when you were writing that, what were the conversations like about how weird or unconventional a main character who’s a woman could be?
Meriwether: Yeah. The notes I got were, like—the first pilot I wrote was called Sluts. It was kind of Girls before Girls, in a way. It was three girls in New York who just, like, had a lot of sex and just were deciding to get their lives together and sort of stop having so much sex. And this was for Fox. It was never gonna get on the air. But that was the first pilot that I wrote, and I had conversations with executives that were like, She either is smart, or she likes sex, and that was a binary thing that I had to genuinely have a conversation with somebody about, where I was like, No, you can be smart and also have had a lot of sex.
Rosin: So you were in your 20s when you wrote that pilot, when you wrote Sluts.
Meriwether: Yeah, I was, like, 25 or something. Yeah.
Rosin: And did you already know, I’m trying to push against some kind of tropes or ideas of how female characters should be?
Meriwether: Yeah. I mean, I think I’ve always come from a place of, like, I’m gonna make jokes about it or try to come at it from a little bit of a sneakier place. I’ve never been a writer that’s been very I have a big statement I wanna make. Which is, honestly, why this show kinda scared me a little bit, because I was like, I don’t get to hide as much.
I don’t get to kind of, like, you know, tap-dance and make jokes and say, like, No, look over here. Look over here. Look over here. But yes, I’ve always been interested in trying to put women on screen that are not what you have seen before. That’s been something that I’ve been interested in for a long time.
I just feel like we’ve taken steps forward and steps back over the past 15 years, but there’s definitely more complicated female characters on television now than there was back then.
When New Girl first aired, I did a lot of press. It was, like, me and Whitney Cummings had comedies coming out, and [people] were like, We can’t believe there are, like, comedies written by women—more than one comedy written by women.
That was like the main thrust of the press. And that would never be a story nowadays. So yes, there, I mean, there is growth. I think that there’s also a lot of moving forward then moving backwards.
Rosin: Yeah. For this episode, we also interviewed my Atlantic colleague Sophie Gilbert, who wrote this book Girl on Girl, which is about how pop culture of the late ’90s and aughts hated women or taught Millennial women to hate themselves.
And I was thinking about you because you, that’s your era of pop culture. I also saw that you signed on to write the biopic of Britney Spears, who is the ultimate example of how the late ’90s and early aughts chewed some women up. And so I wondered if that was part of what motivates you or what excites you about these kinds of projects.
Meriwether: I think so. Yeah. I mean, I do kinda just keep my head down and keep moving forward. Like, I don’t go from a place of like I have an agenda. But yes, those are the characters that really excite me—the women where it’s, like, very hard to put into words how you feel about them. You don’t know if you’re rooting for them or not. I do think it’s a very interesting, fun place to be as a writer, maybe because of all of the notes I got about likability and the desire to sort of get away from that. But I also think it’s not interesting to make somebody completely evil. I think that middle space is really interesting.
Rosin: And maybe it just feels more true.
Meriwether: Yeah. There’s also a tendency to, say, victimize women in a different way, where it’s like they had no agency in what happened to them or, you know, they are completely products of a broken system, which I feel like is not fair either and a little bit patronizing and boring, honestly. So I think I’m interested in, like, all the nuances of why people do the things they do.
[Music]
Rosin: Sophie, you know what I was thinking about? The Olivia Rodrigo reprisal of Lilith Fair.
Olivia Rodrigo: 45,000 people at this festival tonight. Can you believe it?
Rosin: I don’t know if you saw the documentary about Lilith Fair.
Gilbert: I did, yeah.
Rosin: So I watched that documentary, and I think I might have cried, honestly, because I thought, Oh, well, that era is dead. Like, We will never, ever have that back again.
[Sounds from the Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery trailer]
Rosin: A sort of collection of women getting together, talking about their music, entirely made for and run by women, and yet here it is reprised this summer. And I thought, Oh, maybe the sense of agency that’s emerging, it does feel different than what you wrote about [in your book]. It does feel different than the Britney Spears era, the era in which women died by those cultural stories. Now it feels like they’re writing the stories, and so even though they might be grim or they might be inspirational, they are controlling the narrative.
Gilbert: That Lilith documentary was so good and I think so sad, for exactly the reasons that you said, which was: It seemed the last moment when this idea of a women-centric society, or at least an alternative society, seemed possible. (Laughs.) And then everything that happened afterwards in the 2000s, and just this real decade of victimizing women for living their lives in public.
But yes, again, we have this moment of a mainstream pop star holding a massive music festival for abortion-rights charities and reproductive rights, which you can’t imagine someone like Taylor Swift doing that.
Rodrigo: Today I’m so aware of all the women who came before me, who fought for me to enjoy the rights that I enjoy today.
Gilbert: All right, it’s not as subversive and as edgy as what riot-grrrl musicians were doing in the ’90s, but it’s political. It’s active. It’s angry about the way that things are, and it’s willing to take a stand to change them. And then it also—I think the thing that I found so fascinating about this festival, Daisy Chain, was that it just demonstrates the power that women have in the music industry.
Of all the different cultural industries, music really seems to be one where women are dominant right now—where they sell the most records, where they’re making the most interesting music, where they’re the ones that we are drawn to. They have these huge tours, and they have this huge fandom, and they are front and center in music and powerful in a way that men are not. And that, I think, is interesting right now, in this moment. And the question of why, I don’t know. But if we’re looking for things to be hopeful about, that’s definitely one.
Rosin: Right, ’cause in thinking about women’s anger, I got stuck in a kind of limited narrative, which is, Oh, in 2017, women were able to channel the anger in a productive direction. People told their stories. Sort of a dam burst open. There were truths out there, and that was cathartic. And in 2026, we get a serial killer. So then I was trying to think, Well, maybe that’s not that simple. There are places that anger finds an out that are more joyful or productive, and so this is one that I look to.
Gilbert: Yeah. Olivia Rodrigo just released a song called “Serena Joy,” which is named, obviously, after the character in The Handmaid’s Tale who has helped subjugate other women. One of the lyrics in it is, “If you can’t throw a punch, you can learn how to spit.”
[“Serena Joy,” by Olivia Rodrigo]
Gilbert: Just, it’s this idea that numbness is not inevitable. We don’t have to just be complacent forever and ever and ever while our rights are eroded and things are taken away—that in some ways, cultural power is still there, and that there are still women sort of taking a stand for things, and in some ways, storytelling is able to do such interesting work now because we are in a different place than we were in 2017, and we’re much more open to ideas about what’s possible, even if it doesn’t seem like it’s easily achievable.
Rosin: Yeah. Well, Sophie, thank you so much for talking this through with me today.
Gilbert: Oh, it’s a pleasure. Thank you for having me.
[Music]
Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West with help from Jacob Smollen. It was edited by Claudine Ebeid. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.
Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.
I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

articles.title: Lời khai ban đầu của nghi can sát hại 3 người ở Đồng Nai
articles.text:
Ngày 3/9, Công an TP Đồng Nai cho biết, Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an TP Đồng Nai đang giám sát nghiêm ngặt đối với Nguyễn Đức Anh (SN 2005, ngụ phường Hố Nai, TP Đồng Nai). Đây là nghi can trong vụ án mạng khiến 3 người tử vong, 1 người bị thương xảy ra rạng sáng 3/9 tại ấp Bùi Chu, xã Bình Minh, TP Đồng Nai.
Theo cơ quan công an, vụ việc xảy ra vào khoảng 1h45 ngày 3/9. Sau khi gây án, Nguyễn Đức Anh bị nhiều vết thương và đang được điều trị tại cơ sở y tế dưới sự giám sát của lực lượng chức năng. Bước đầu, Đức Anh khai nhận có quan hệ tình cảm với Đ.T.P.A (SN 2009). Gần đây, P.A nói lời chia tay nên Đức Anh nảy sinh ý định sát hại bạn gái.
Rạng sáng 3/9, sau khi uống rượu cùng một nhóm bạn, Đức Anh mang theo dao đến nhà P.A. Tuy nhiên, do cửa nhà đã khóa, Đức Anh trèo lên mái, cạy ô cửa giếng trời để tìm cách đột nhập.
Thời điểm này, anh Đ.V.R (cha của P.A) nghe tiếng động nên bật điện kiểm tra và nói chuyện với Đức Anh. Tuy nhiên, Đức Anh vẫn tiếp tục cạy ô cửa giếng trời, đồng thời đe dọa sẽ sát hại cả gia đình. Lo sợ, anh R chốt chặt các cửa trong nhà. Không thể đột nhập vào nhà P.A, Đức Anh trèo qua mái nhà anh N.V.Q (SN 1986), nằm sát bên, rồi mở cửa tầng 2 để vào bên trong.
Phát hiện có người đột nhập, anh Q ra kiểm tra và thấy Đức Anh đang đi xuống cầu thang nên Đức Anh lập tức cầm dao lao vào tấn công anh Q. Thấy vậy, anh Q chạy xuống khu vực bếp lấy dao chống trả nhưng bị Đức Anh đâm trọng thương nên anh này mở cửa chạy ra đường nhưng Đức Anh tiếp tục đuổi theo tấn công cho đến khi nạn nhân gục xuống.
Sau đó, Đức Anh quay trở lại nhà, chốt cổng rồi xông vào phòng ngủ, tấn công chị H.T.M (SN 1990 vợ anh Q) cùng hai con của anh Q là N.T.H (SN 2015) và N.N.H (SN 2025). Hậu quả, chị M cùng hai cháu T.H và N.H tử vong. Riêng anh Q bị thương nặng, đang được cấp cứu, điều trị.
Trong khi đó, anh Đ.V.R đã gọi điện trình báo Công an xã Bình Minh. Khi lực lượng công an đến hiện trường, Đức Anh mở cổng và bị khống chế, bắt giữ.
Theo lời khai ban đầu, Đức Anh cho biết không quen biết và không có mâu thuẫn với gia đình anh Q và các nạn nhân. Ngay sau khi xảy ra vụ việc, Phòng Cảnh sát hình sự Công an thành phố Đồng Nai phối hợp Công an xã Bình Minh, Phòng Kỹ thuật hình sự Công an thành phố, Viện KSND TP Đồng Nai và Viện KSND Khu vực 3 tiến hành khám nghiệm hiện trường, khám nghiệm tử thi, lấy lời khai nhân chứng và những người liên quan.
Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an thành phố Đồng Nai đang tiếp tục điều tra, làm rõ nguyên nhân, diễn biến vụ án và các tình tiết liên quan.

articles.title: Nhiều dự án 'mắc kẹt' ở Đắk Lắk được khơi thông sau 45 ngày đêm gỡ mặt bằng
articles.text:
Chiều 3/9, UBND tỉnh Đắk Lắk tổ chức Hội nghị tổng kết Chiến dịch 45 ngày đêm đẩy nhanh tiến độ giải phóng mặt bằng (GPMB) các dự án trọng điểm trên địa bàn tỉnh.
Phát biểu tại hội nghị, Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Đắk Lắk Đỗ Hữu Huy cho biết GPMB được xác định là một trong những “điểm nghẽn của điểm nghẽn” trong triển khai các dự án đầu tư công, ảnh hưởng trực tiếp đến tiến độ giải ngân và mục tiêu tăng trưởng hai con số của tỉnh.
Từ 42 dự án ban đầu, chiến dịch được mở rộng lên 53 dự án, công trình trọng điểm, với mục tiêu phấn đấu hoàn thành tối thiểu 90-95% khối lượng GPMB. Năm tổ công tác do các đồng chí lãnh đạo Tỉnh ủy làm tổ trưởng được thành lập, trực tiếp xuống địa bàn chỉ đạo, đôn đốc, tháo gỡ từng vướng mắc.
Sau 45 ngày đêm triển khai với tinh thần “không kể ngày đêm, không kể thứ Bảy, Chủ nhật”, 7 dự án đã hoàn thành 100% GPMB. Trong đó có Dự án thành phần 3 - cao tốc Khánh Hòa - Buôn Ma Thuột, Bến cảng Bãi Gốc, Đường giao thông Cảng Bãi Gốc đi Khu kinh tế Vân Phong và các gói thầu hồ chứa nước Ea Súp Thượng.
Ngoài ra, 15 dự án khác đạt trên 90%, nhiều dự án vượt 95% như: Đường liên huyện Cư M’gar - Ea H’leo đạt 97,84%; Hồ Suối Cái đạt 99,60%; tuyến đường bộ ven biển đoạn Bắc cầu An Hải đạt 98,66%; hợp phần bồi thường, di dân hồ Krông Pách Thượng giai đoạn 1 đạt 97,95%...
Đáng chú ý, nhiều dự án tồn đọng kéo dài nhiều năm, tưởng chừng bế tắc như: cơ sở hạ tầng trung tâm điểm du lịch hồ Lắk, Đường Ama Jhao nối dài, Đường Tôn Đức Thắng, Kênh hồ Ia M’rơ giai đoạn 2… đã có chuyển biến rõ rệt.
Theo ông Đỗ Hữu Huy, điểm khác biệt của chiến dịch là các tổ công tác chuyển từ cách làm “quản lý hành chính” sang “chỉ đạo tại hiện trường”, trực tiếp bóc tách từng điểm nghẽn về pháp lý, thủ tục và vận động người dân.
Ông Lương Nguyễn Minh Triết - Bí thư Tỉnh ủy, Trưởng Đoàn đại biểu Quốc hội tỉnh Đắk Lắk, đánh giá cao kết quả đạt được sau 45 ngày đêm triển khai chiến dịch.
Theo Bí thư Tỉnh ủy Đắk Lắk, việc 7 dự án hoàn thành 100% GPMB, 15 dự án đạt trên 90%, trong đó 9 dự án vượt 95%, cho thấy những vấn đề tưởng chừng kéo dài, phức tạp vẫn có thể được tháo gỡ khi cả hệ thống chính trị cùng vào cuộc, quyết liệt và bám sát cơ sở.
Tuy nhiên, ông Lương Nguyễn Minh Triết cho rằng, kết quả đạt được mới là bước khởi đầu, bởi vẫn còn 21 dự án chưa đạt 90% GPMB, một số dự án có tiến độ rất thấp. Nguyên nhân không chỉ nằm ở nguồn gốc đất phức tạp, giá bồi thường chưa sát thị trường mà còn có những hạn chế chủ quan như xác minh nguồn gốc đất chậm, trách nhiệm người đứng đầu chưa đồng đều, hạ tầng điện, nước tại một số khu tái định cư chưa đáp ứng yêu cầu.
Bí thư Tỉnh ủy Đắk Lắk lưu ý, có nơi mặt bằng đã được bàn giao nhưng dự án vẫn chưa chuyển động tương xứng khi chủ đầu tư chậm đôn đốc, nhà thầu chưa huy động đủ máy móc, nhân lực. Vì vậy, ông yêu cầu tiếp tục gắn trách nhiệm người đứng đầu với kết quả GPMB, tăng cường kiểm tra thực địa và đặc biệt phải gắn GPMB với tiến độ thi công.
Bí thư Tỉnh ủy Đắk Lắk Lương Nguyễn Minh Triết nhấn mạnh: “Chiến dịch 45 ngày đêm đã khép lại về mặt thời gian, nhưng tinh thần chiến dịch thì không được phép dừng lại”.

articles.title: Vĩnh Long: Lấy mẫu ADN tại 390 phần mộ ở Nghĩa trang liệt sĩ Giồng Trôm
articles.text:
Theo kế hoạch, Bộ Chỉ huy quân sự tỉnh sẽ tổ chức lấy mẫu tại 390 phần mộ liệt sĩ chưa xác định được thông tin đang được an táng tại Nghĩa trang liệt sĩ Giồng Trôm.
Công tác lấy mẫu ADN được tổ chức thành 2 đội, mỗi đội dự kiến thực hiện khoảng 20 phần mộ/ngày. Các lực lượng sẽ triển khai liên tục cho đến khi hoàn thành việc lấy mẫu tại toàn bộ số phần mộ.
Quá trình thực hiện gặp một số khó khăn do nhiều phần mộ đã được nâng cấp, gia cố, gây trở ngại cho việc tiếp cận và lấy mẫu. Tuy nhiên, các lực lượng tham gia vẫn nỗ lực khắc phục, bảo đảm yêu cầu chuyên môn, đồng thời đẩy nhanh tiến độ để sớm hoàn thành nhiệm vụ.
Việc lấy mẫu hài cốt tại các phần mộ chưa xác định được thông tin là cơ sở phục vụ công tác giám định, xác định danh tính liệt sĩ, góp phần cung cấp thông tin cho thân nhân và thực hiện tốt công tác đền ơn đáp nghĩa.
Theo thống kê, Nghĩa trang liệt sĩ Giồng Trôm hiện có 2.741 phần mộ. Trong đó, 326 phần mộ thiếu thông tin và 613 phần mộ chưa xác định được thông tin.
Thực hiện Chiến dịch "500 ngày đêm thực hiện tìm kiếm, quy tập và xác định danh tính hài cốt liệt sĩ", đến nay, tỉnh Vĩnh Long đã hoàn thành lấy 1.786 mẫu ADN tại 2.009 phần mộ. Trong số này, 1.346 mẫu đã được bàn giao về Viện Khoa học hình sự, Bộ Công an để phục vụ công tác xác định danh tính hài cốt liệt sĩ còn thiếu thông tin.

articles.title: How ‘Somatics’ Became the Solution to Modern Life
articles.text:
How ‘Somatics’ Became the Solution to Modern Life
The word isn’t new—but lately, it’s everywhere.
When clients go to Sybil Ottenstein for therapy, they tend to arrive with answers. Many of them have seen shrinks before. They can tell her which events from their past were formative, and point to the ripple effects in their current life. They’re like detectives, she told me, with all the dots connected on their corkboard of evidence. Intellectually, they’ve cracked the case. The problem is that they don’t feel any better.
That’s why they’re seeking something different from Ottenstein: somatic psychotherapy. Traditional talk therapy could be seen as a top-down approach. You identify problems in your thinking, your habits, or your life, and hope that by working through them, you can resolve physical manifestations of emotional issues—the chest palpitations of anxiety, the stomachache of stress. Somatic therapy, by contrast, works from the bottom up. Ottenstein typically starts her sessions by asking clients to slow down and pay attention to corporeal sensations: “What does it feel like in your chest? In your throat?” As they talk, she encourages them to stay in their body, to let themselves feel whatever is coming up. People cry. They yawn. They scream. They stretch. They dance.
The word somatic, according to Merriam-Webster, merely means “of, relating to, or affecting the body.” But recently, it’s been popping up everywhere, appended to a variety of practices that involve tuning in to physical symptoms in order to ameliorate psychological ones. Somatic therapists like Ottenstein have noticed a significant bump in interest; one of the major somatic-therapy training programs reported that its applicants more than doubled from 2020 to 2023. Other practitioners offer somatic dance, somatic yoga, somatic workouts. (The terms seem a touch redundant.)
On Instagram, hundreds of thousands of posts appear with the hashtag #somatic. A “somatic exercise” trainer who goes by the “Workout Witch” (nearly 2 million followers) teaches small, repetitive movements meant to discharge negative feelings—curl your head down for “sorrow/despair,” pull your right ear for “overwhelm”—and promises that “trauma can be released from your hips.” All over my feed, fit young women are humming, hitting their sternum, pinching their nose bridge, and bouncing their knees all the way to inner peace.
Much of the time, as with many other wellness ventures, someone stands to make money. At one somatic-workout class I attended, where a staffer told me that the goal was to “move stagnant energy out,” the lobby featured a gift-shop corner with jewelry, T-shirts, and $65 “body gloss” from a brand called Oui the People. But clearly, plenty of Americans are willing to pay for the promise of a psychic cleanse. Practitioners refer to “stuck energy,” to “trapped emotions,” to “resetting” a nervous system caught in fight-or-flight mode. “We have all these ways of just storing that gunk inside,” Ottenstein told me. I pictured, uncomfortably, a thick, black goo running through my veins.
Somatics—the whole roomy umbrella of practices—might seem like an odd fit for the information age, when people are more accustomed to finding answers on the internet than within themselves. But that could be precisely the draw for thinkers and analyzers who are tired of ruminating in anxious circles, who spend their days in front of a laptop and nights scrolling an iPhone. For millennia, people have yearned to break out of the confines of their bodies; they’ve searched—through religion, spirituality, drugs—for transcendence. Now, for some, the existential quest is inverted: Instead of seeking to escape their prison of flesh and bones, they want to reinhabit it.
The origin of somatics is difficult to pinpoint, though it’s certainly not recent. Some credit Wilhelm Reich, a student of Freud’s, who theorized in the early 1900s that patients held tension in their bodies—“muscular armor”—as a subconscious defense against trauma, leading to aches, pains, and inflammation. But it wasn’t until the 1970s that the field began to formalize, developed in part by the American philosophy professor Thomas Hanna, who defined somatics as the study of “the body as perceived from within.” That same decade, a UC Berkeley biophysics doctoral student, Peter Levine, developed “somatic experiencing”: a therapeutic method based on the idea that people, like other animals, react to trauma with a flight, fight, or freeze response, powered by a burst of adrenaline. After the source of danger is gone, Levine argued, they have pent-up “survival energy” to unleash: They need to physically shake it off. He pointed to videos of impalas, quaking and buckling after surviving a cheetah attack. When humans go through something upsetting, Ottenstein told me, “we go to work the next day.”
This idea—that trauma is held in the body, and thus must be physically remedied—was once fairly niche. In recent years, though, it has been jolted into prominence. The psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk’s book The Body Keeps the Score, which argues for somatic treatments of PTSD, was first released in 2014 and was not an immediate hit. In 2021, it reached the No. 1 spot on the New York Times best-seller list for paperback nonfiction. And although it has been accused of resting on shaky science, it has continued to dominate the charts for years.
Van der Kolk wrote about violent assaults, wartime atrocities, severe childhood abuse—circumstances that many readers hadn’t directly experienced. Yet The Body Keeps the Score seemed to resonate anyway. When it gained momentum, lots of Americans had spent the previous year safe in their homes, baking bread and taking Zoom calls. (“When people say the pandemic has been a collective trauma,” van der Kolk told The Atlantic that year, “I say, absolutely not.”) Most had also, however, been detached from the rich sensory experience of interacting with the external world. Now here was a book about people who’d felt estranged from their own body—and then, through simple movement, play, and touch, found their way back to their surroundings, and to themselves.
In the years since, most people have emerged from pandemic isolation. Yet the share of Americans who say they frequently experience stress, which has been rising for decades, has continued its upward trend. Talk therapy remains popular, but it’s not always affordable or accessible—and much of the time, it doesn’t take physical symptoms into account. Meanwhile, many medical doctors don’t consider psychological causes of physical ailments. Stress in particular is “like this mythical creature,” Aditi Nerurkar, a physician at Harvard Medical School, told me. “And we don’t have a lot of time. We have to focus on your hemoglobin. Did you get a mammogram? Did you get a pap smear? What is your cholesterol?”
No wonder, then, that somatics is a flourishing industry. Many Americans already distrust medical institutions; maybe they want to bypass the dismissive doctor, or the therapist who wants to rehash every daddy issue but can’t seem to fix anything. So they turn to this strange constellation of New Age–y courses, TikTok sages, and licensed counselors. Some offerings target people with capital-T Trauma; others claim to be for just about anyone. Many present themselves as alternatives to more traditional paths to mental well-being. The question is whether they can really help the frazzled masses.
Somatics does get a lot of things right. Plenty of bodily sensations are, at root, psychological. Some communication does need to happen between the brain and the rest of the body. That’s how you know to respond to danger: The amygdala triggers the nervous system to increase your heart rate, deliver more blood to muscles, and release a flood of adrenaline. When I spoke with Nerurkar, she rattled off an incomplete list of physical symptoms that might result from stress: headaches, dizziness, nausea, vision changes. When she was in residency training, she said, she experienced what felt like a “stampede of wild horses” across her chest and was convinced that she had a heart problem—until her doctors, having conducted a battery of tests, recommended that she seriously consider chilling out.
And many components of somatic practice have evidence to back them up. Interoception, or awareness of one’s own physical signals, really can be important for well-being—perhaps because it increases people’s sense of attunement with their body, connection with the present moment, or agency over otherwise vague and inscrutable sensations. Mindfulness meditation, which involves interoception, has been shown to decrease stress and anxiety and even reduce physical pain. Yoga and breathing exercises can decrease amygdala activation and lead to better concentration, memory, and executive function.
But the somatics packaging of these techniques is alluring partly because of the emotional liberation it promises. Somaticists tend to describe a clear path: identify a physical signal, connect it to its psychic cause, then let it go. If the nervous system overactivates, surely you can just reset it. If the body holds trauma, surely the body can relinquish it.
These were always just metaphors, though, and imperfect ones. The amygdala doesn’t have a reboot button. There is no viscous gunk of emotional pain to flush out. The Body Keeps the Score has been somewhat debunked; critics have argued that van der Kolk incorrectly described certain studies, and that he seems to have made up others entirely. (Responding to the writer Emi Nietfeld’s critique in Mother Jones, van der Kolk said that at times he drew on unpublished data.) Trauma experts have pushed back on his wholesale condemnation of talk therapy, which can be, according to a mountain of evidence, very helpful for treating PTSD. There’s also something ironic in how certain somaticists—ostensibly advocates for the mind-body connection—talk as if the two are separated by a nearly unbridgeable gap: the physical burden of trauma unreachable through thinking or conversation, and perhaps not even accessible to conscious awareness.
So somatics isn’t a miracle cure. And it’s probably right to be skeptical of influencers who seek to collect on people’s need to feel at home in their body. But that doesn’t mean somatics can’t be helpful. Much of it, after all, turns out to be pretty straightforward. Movement is good, generally. Breathing is good. Stepping away from your screen—stretching your limbs, remembering you are real and tangible and mortal—is good.
When I signed up for that somatic-exercise class, I expected that I might leave rolling my eyes, but I secretly hoped I’d walk out lighter, more alive and connected to myself and the world. What I found was something in between. The actual workout couldn’t have been more basic: It consisted largely of squats, jumping jacks, crunches, some yoga—downward dog, child’s pose. Occasionally the instructor would remind us to check in with our bodies: “What are you being invited into? And I don’t mean the burpee.” Or: “Let the chin enter the conversation.” Otherwise it hardly seemed uniquely somatic, or uniquely anything.
Then again, I had the post-workout endorphin glow. I’d left my apartment and shut my phone in a locker. An hour later, I exited the studio somewhat baffled. But walking out onto a busy Manhattan street, I felt a little more conscious of the sun on my cheek, the solidness of the ground pushing against my feet. This was silly, I thought. And also: Maybe I’ll come back.

articles.title: Vụ cháy nhà 4 tầng ở Nha Trang: Hai nạn nhân tử vong
articles.text:
Ngày 3/9, lãnh đạo UBND phường Nam Nha Trang đã đến thăm hỏi, chia buồn, động viên và trao hỗ trợ 50 triệu đồng cho gia đình hai nạn nhân trong vụ cháy căn nhà 4 tầng tại Khu đô thị An Bình Tân, phường Nam Nha Trang.
Khoảng 11h ngày 2/9, đám cháy bất ngờ bùng phát tại tầng 2 của căn nhà trên đường T7, Khu đô thị An Bình Tân, sau đó nhanh chóng lan lên các tầng phía trên.
Nhận được tin báo, lực lượng chức năng khẩn trương có mặt, triển khai các phương án chữa cháy. Sau nhiều phút nỗ lực, đám cháy được dập tắt hoàn toàn.
Thời điểm xảy ra cháy, trong nhà có 6 người. Bốn người tự thoát ra ngoài an toàn, trong khi hai người bị mắc kẹt bên trong. Lực lượng chữa cháy chuyên nghiệp phối hợp với ê-kíp y, bác sĩ Trung tâm Cấp cứu 115 tỉnh Khánh Hòa sử dụng thiết bị chuyên dụng tiếp cận, giải cứu hai nạn nhân là bà L.T.K. (74 tuổi) và bà L.N.H.C. (42 tuổi).
Theo Bệnh viện Đa khoa tỉnh Khánh Hòa, khi được đưa đến bệnh viện cấp cứu, cả hai nạn nhân đều trong tình trạng tiên lượng rất nặng.
Cụ thể, bà L.T.K. được chẩn đoán ngưng tuần hoàn, hô hấp ngoại viện do ngạt khói cháy, bỏng độ 2, có di chứng tai biến mạch máu não và phải thở máy. Bà L.N.H.C. bị ngưng hô hấp, tuần hoàn, bỏng hô hấp và bỏng toàn thân độ 2.
Sau đó, tình trạng bà L.N.H.C. diễn biến nặng. Gia đình xin đưa bệnh nhân về nhà để lo hậu sự. Đến trưa 3/9, bà L.T.K.C. tử vong.
Công an phường Nam Nha Trang đã phối hợp với các đơn vị liên quan khám nghiệm hiện trường, đồng thời tiếp tục điều tra, làm rõ nguyên nhân vụ cháy.

articles.title: Khơi thông "mạch máu" giao thông qua Đồng Tháp đi miền Tây
articles.text:
Xác định giao thông đi trước mở đường, tỉnh Đồng Tháp đang huy động các nguồn lực để triển khai nhiều dự án giao thông trọng điểm. Các tuyến liên kết vùng được kỳ vọng sẽ tạo động lực mới trong phát triển kinh tế - xã hội của Đồng Tháp và các tỉnh miền Tây.
Cao tốc, QL1 đều quá tải
Nhiều năm qua phương tiện vận chuyển hàng hóa, hành khách từ TP.HCM đi các tỉnh miền Tây chủ yếu lưu thông trên hai trục giao thông xương sống, gồm: cao tốc TP.HCM - Mỹ Thuận và quốc lộ 1 (QL1). Tuy nhiên, hai trục đường được xem là huyết mạch hiện đã quá tải.
Minh chứng rõ nhất vào các dịp cao điểm cuối tuần, lễ, Tết dòng xe cộ nhích từng mét một trên đường chật chội, quá tải trở thành hình ảnh dễ thấy. Tỉnh Đồng Tháp với vai trò cửa ngõ luôn chịu áp lực giao thông rất lớn.
Nhận thấy giao thông vẫn là nút thắt cần sớm được tháo gỡ, UBND tỉnh Đồng Tháp, đã xác định trong giai đoạn 2025 - 2030 đột phá hạ tầng giao thông là một trong những ưu tiên hàng đầu.
Tỉnh sẽ tập trung nguồn lực đầu tư, huy động phát triển hệ thống kết cấu hạ tầng giao thông đồng bộ, khơi thông kết nối vùng và nội tỉnh để thu hút nhà đầu tư chiến lược, tạo động lực phát triển kinh tế, xã hội.
Đồng Tháp sẽ ưu tiên triển khai các công trình trọng điểm kết nối TP.HCM, Tây Ninh đi các tỉnh Đồng bằng sông Cửu Long. Đây là một trong những khâu đột phá chiến lược của tỉnh trong thời gian tới.
Để hiện thực hóa mục tiêu này, tỉnh sẽ tập trung mọi nguồn lực, phối hợp chặt chẽ với Trung ương sớm hoàn thành các tuyến cao tốc như: Cao Lãnh - An Hữu, Mỹ An - Cao Lãnh, mở rộng cao tốc TP.HCM - Trung Lương - Mỹ Thuận, đẩy nhanh chuẩn bị đầu tư các dự án giao thông liên kết vùng.
Tháo gỡ điểm nghẽn giao thông
Theo ông Nguyễn Trường Giang, Trưởng phòng kế hoạch tài chính Sở Xây dựng tỉnh Đồng Tháp, đầu tháng 8/2026, UBND tỉnh đã chấp thuận chủ trương cho lập báo cáo nghiên cứu tiền khả thi dự án kết nối liên vùng tỉnh Đồng Tháp, gồm 7 dự án thành phần.
Các dự án liên kết vùng gồm: Trục giao thông đô thị TP.HCM - Tây Ninh - Đồng Tháp (quy hoạch QL50B), đường 877C (nối QL1 - QL50 đến cao tốc TP.HCM - Trung Lương), QL30B, đường 870B (từ QL1 đến đường 878). Mở rộng QL50, QL60, QL30, đầu tư đường ĐT845 kết nối các tuyến ĐT861, 863.
Tỉnh xác định rõ phát triển hạ tầng giao thông đồng bộ hiện đại, thích ứng với biến đổi khí hậu, chú trọng xây dựng hạ tầng giao thông đầu mối kết nối hạ tầng logistics xuyên biên giới và đa phương thức.
Ông Nguyễn Thế Hồng Trung, Giám đốc Sở Xây dựng tỉnh Đồng Tháp cho biết, mới đây (tháng 7/2026), Tỉnh ủy đã thông qua Nghị quyết về phát triển hạ tầng giao thông tỉnh giai đoạn 2026 - 2030. Trong đó, xác định rõ với mục tiêu hướng đến tỉnh Đồng Tháp trở thành trung tâm trung chuyển của tiểu vùng sông Mê Kông.
Phấn đấu đến năm 2030 đầu tư xây dựng thêm 124km đường cao tốc, 30km đường quốc lộ và 200km đường tỉnh, đầu tư nâng cấp khoảng 20,8km đường thủy nội địa quốc gia. Ưu tiên đầu tư hình thành hai tuyến đường bộ kết nối Đông - Tây nối từ khu biển Gò Công đến cửa khẩu Dinh Bà và từ biển Tân Thành với cửa khẩu Quốc tế Thường Phước.
Song song đó là phối hợp kêu gọi đầu tư hệ thống cảng biển, cảng hàng hóa và hành khách ở sông Tiền, sông Hậu, sông Soài Rạp. Đồng thời, phát triển phương tiện vận tải chất lượng cao, từng bước chuyển đổi phương tiện theo hướng xanh, sử dụng năng lượng thân thiện với môi trường.
Trên lĩnh vực đường sắt, Đồng Tháp sẵn sàng phối hợp các bộ, ngành Trung ương và TP.HCM đầu tư tuyến đường sắt tốc độ cao TP.HCM - Cần Thơ nhằm tận dụng cơ hội phát triển các đô thị, giảm chi phí logistics, thu hút đầu tư, phát triển công nghiệp, dịch vụ, tạo động lực phát triển kinh tế, xã hội toàn vùng.
Tháng 7/2026, UBND tỉnh Đồng Tháp đã ban hành Kế hoạch triển khai thực hiện phát triển các khu công nghiệp (KCN) trên địa bàn tỉnh Đồng Tháp giai đoạn 2026 - 2030. Đồng Tháp sẽ có thêm 18 KCN mới đến năm 2030 với diện tích khoảng 4.912 ha. Hiện có bốn khu đang đầu tư xây dựng,
Tỉnh đang kêu gọi đầu tư thêm 14 Khu công nghiệp với diện tích 3.799ha, theo phương hướng phát triển trong điều chỉnh Quy hoạch tỉnh Đồng Tháp thời kỳ 2021 - 2030, tầm nhìn đến năm 2050.
